person.name: Friedensreich_Hundertwasser
person.summary: Friedensreich Hundertwasser (born Friedrich Stowasser) was an Austrian artist best known for his vividly colored, organic paintings and his unconventional architectural designs that rejected straight lines and embraced nature. A Holocaust survivor from Vienna, he developed an international career in postwar Europe, formulated his own artistic philosophy of 'transautomatism', and became a pioneer of green architecture and environmental activism. From the 1970s onward he lived between Europe and New Zealand, where he realized large-scale ecological and architectural projects until his death in 2000.

chapters.headline: Early Life and Artistic Awakening
chapters.description: Childhood in Vienna, survival under Nazism, and first steps toward an artistic identity after the war.

chapters.headline: Avant‑Garde and International Breakthrough
chapters.description: Immersion in European avant‑garde circles, formulation of his own artistic philosophy, and rising international recognition.

chapters.headline: Nature, Architecture and Alternative Living
chapters.description: Withdrawal into nature, the turn toward architectural work, and the creation of self‑sufficient rural and maritime bases.

chapters.headline: Public Icon and Global Projects
chapters.description: High‑profile architecture, environmental campaigns, and late projects spanning Europe, Japan, and New Zealand.

events.title: Birth in Vienna
events.description: Friedrich Stowasser, later known as Friedensreich Hundertwasser, was born in Vienna as the only child of engineer Ernst Stowasser and Elsa Stowasser, née Scheuer, who was of Jewish origin. His early family roots reached into Bohemia on his father’s side and Moravia on his mother’s, embedding him in the multicultural fabric of Central Europe.

events.title: Father’s early death
events.description: Shortly after his first birthday, Hundertwasser’s father died from appendicitis, leaving his mother to raise him alone in interwar Vienna. This early loss meant a childhood marked by emotional and economic vulnerability, deepening his later attachment to his mother and his sense of being an outsider.

events.title: Montessori schooling and baptism
events.description: At about seven he entered a Montessori school in Vienna, where art teachers noticed his extraordinary feeling for form and color, encouraging his early creative impulses. That same year he was baptized Catholic, a step that, amid rising antisemitism, also had the pragmatic dimension of partially masking his maternal Jewish heritage.

events.date_note: Attended winter semester 1948/49 for about three months
events.title: Brief study at Vienna Academy
events.description: After completing his Matura at the Bundesgymnasium Horn, Hundertwasser enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna for the winter semester 1948/49. He left after about three months, but during this short time he began signing his works with the name "Hundertwasser", derived from the Slavic word for "hundred" and marking his first decisive act of self‑invention as an artist.

locations.name_historic: Akademie der bildenden Künste Wien, Wien
locations.name_modern: Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, Vienna, Austria

images.caption: Textile design by Friedensreich Hundertwasser for Fernwärme Wien AG, illustrating his later mature style developed long after his brief studies at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna in 1948/49.

events.date_note: Covers first Italy journey in 1949 and subsequent travels to Paris and North Africa 1950–1951
events.title: Formative travels to South and North
events.description: Leaving academic study behind, Hundertwasser traveled to Italy in April 1949, then on to Paris with the French artist René Brô, and in 1951 continued alone to Morocco, Tunisia, and Sicily. Encounters with Mediterranean light, North African landscapes, and the works of artists such as Egon Schiele, Paul Klee, and Walter Kampmann profoundly shaped his watercolor style and his lifelong focus on trees, vegetation, and a "ensouled" nature.

images.caption: Exhibition of Friedensreich Hundertwasser’s paintings and graphic works, showing the mature style whose roots lie in his formative travels and watercolor experiments around 1949–1951.

events.title: First major exhibitions
events.description: In the early 1950s Hundertwasser began exhibiting his paintings, first in Vienna in 1952 and 1953, then in Milan and in the Galerie Facchetti in Paris in 1954 and 1956. These shows brought his spiraling, intensely colored works to an international audience for the first time and established him within the postwar European avant‑garde.

images.caption: Exhibition of Friedensreich Hundertwasser paintings and graphics at Forum Würth Arlesheim, showing his colorful, spiraling works similar in style to those first exhibited internationally in the early 1950s.

events.title: Buys Norman farm and marries
events.description: In 1957 Hundertwasser bought a farmhouse on the edge of Normandy, creating a rural base outside Paris that suited his solitary temperament and love of nature. The following year he married the 16‑year‑old Herta Leitner in Gibraltar, a brief union that ended in divorce after two years but marked his first attempt to combine an itinerant artist’s life with conventional domesticity.

events.title: Hamburg ‘Endless Line’ action
events.description: Invited as a guest lecturer to the Hochschule für bildende Künste in Hamburg, Hundertwasser staged an action in December 1959 with Bazon Brock, Herbert Schuldt, and students, drawing a continuous, meandering line through his classroom. When the conservative director forced them to stop, Hundertwasser resigned his post, dramatizing his rejection of straight lines and institutional constraints.

locations.name_historic: Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg, Hamburg, West Germany
locations.name_modern: Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany

events.title: Japan prize and second marriage
events.description: In 1961 Hundertwasser traveled to Japan and received the Mainichi Prize at the 6th International Art Exhibition in Tokyo, deepening his fascination with East Asian culture. The following year he married the Japanese woman Yuko Ikewada, a relationship intertwined with his experiments in translating his given name Friedrich into Japanese characters that eventually led to his artistic forename "Friedensreich"; the marriage ended in 1966.

images.caption: Cloth (furoshiki) designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating his characteristic use of color and pattern influenced in part by his interest in Japanese art and culture.

events.title: Breakthrough retrospectives in Europe
events.description: From 1962 onward Hundertwasser’s work was presented in major retrospectives, beginning with a large show in the Austrian pavilion at the Venice Biennale and followed by a traveling exhibition organized by the Kestner‑Gesellschaft in Hannover. Shown in cities such as Amsterdam, Bern, Stockholm, and Vienna, and accompanied by his first catalogue raisonné, these exhibitions consolidated his status as a leading figure of postwar European art.

locations.name_historic: Austrian Pavilion, Giardini della Biennale, Venice
locations.name_modern: Giardini della Biennale, Venice, Veneto, Italy

images.caption: Exhibition of works by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating the type of retrospective displays that helped establish his reputation in Europe from the early 1960s onward.

events.title: Retreat to Waldviertel ‘Hahnsäge’
events.description: Seeking distance from urban life, Hundertwasser purchased the disused sawmill "Hahnsäge" in the thinly populated Waldviertel region of Lower Austria in 1966. He converted the secluded property into a personal refuge, integrating living and working spaces into the surrounding forest landscape—a concrete step toward the symbiosis of dwelling and nature that would define his later architecture.

locations.name_modern: Hahnsäge, near Zwettl, Waldviertel, Lower Austria, Austria

events.title: Film ‘Hundertwassers Regentag’
events.description: Between 1970 and 1972 Hundertwasser collaborated with director Peter Schamoni on the film "Hundertwassers Regentag", centered on the old cargo ship he had sailed from Sicily to Venice and transformed into his floating studio Regentag. The film, following an earlier documentary by Ferry Radax, helped shape his public image as a seafaring, nature‑embracing artist who rejected conventional boundaries between life and art.

images.caption: Textile artwork designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating his characteristic colorful, organic forms similar to those seen in his broader body of work around the time of the film “Hundertwassers Regentag”.

events.title: Establishes New Zealand nature project
events.description: After a museum touring exhibition brought him to New Zealand in 1973, Hundertwasser bought several parcels of land in the Bay of Islands, encompassing the entire Kaurinui Valley. There he planted more than 100,000 native trees, created ponds, canals, and plant‑based sewage systems, and lived in modest structures like a bottle house and mountain hut, realizing his dream of giving land back to nature through ecological design and self‑sufficient living.

locations.name_historic: Kaurinui Valley, Bay of Islands, New Zealand
locations.name_modern: Kaurinui Valley, Bay of Islands, Northland, New Zealand

images.caption: Friedensreich Hundertwasser on his land in New Zealand, where he created an extensive reforestation and ecological living project beginning in the 1970s.

events.title: Pioneer ‘tree tenant’ actions
events.description: In 1975 Hundertwasser participated in the Triennale di Milano, where he installed about 15 "Baummieter" or tree tenants, planting live trees to grow out of windows along a city street and issuing the manifesto "Inquilino Albero". Similar actions in Vienna and Munich in the early 1980s made him an early proponent of façade greening and vertical gardens as a way to reunite architecture and vegetation.

images.caption: The Green Citadel of Magdeburg, a later Hundertwasser-designed building featuring facade greening and vegetation integrated into the architecture, illustrating principles similar to his 1970s "tree tenant" actions.

events.title: Architectural turn and Hundertwasserhaus
events.description: In 1981 Hundertwasser was appointed to head a master class in painting at the Vienna Academy, but his energies increasingly shifted toward architecture, starting with ceramic‑clad factory façades and culminating in the Hundertwasserhaus in Vienna. Laid out in 1983 and handed over to tenants on 17 February 1986, the municipal housing complex, with its irregular floors, colorful surfaces, and rooftop trees, became an international symbol of humane, nature‑integrated urban living.

images.caption: Signboard referencing Friedensreich Hundertwasser at Hundertwasser Station in Uelzen, Germany, reflecting his characteristic colorful architectural style similar to that used in Hundertwasserhaus in Vienna.

events.title: Activism at Hainburger Au
events.description: In 1984 Hundertwasser joined environmental activists occupying the Hainburger Au wetlands to block construction of a power plant on the Danube. Demonstrating in freezing temperatures and dramatically tearing up his recently awarded Grand Austrian State Prize at a press conference, he used his fame to support grassroots ecological protest against state‑backed industrial projects.

locations.name_historic: Hainburger Au, near Hainburg an der Donau, Lower Austria
locations.name_modern: Hainburger Au, Hainburg an der Donau, Lower Austria, Austria

events.title: Opening of KunstHausWien
events.description: On 9 April 1991 the KunstHausWien – Museum Hundertwasser opened in Vienna in a former factory remodeled according to his designs. Housing the only permanent comprehensive exhibition of his work, from early paintings to architecture, alongside contemporary shows, it institutionalized his artistic legacy during his lifetime and turned his organic, colorful aesthetic into a permanent cultural landmark.

images.caption: Textile design by Friedensreich Hundertwasser for Fernwärme Wien AG, reflecting the colorful organic aesthetic also used in his architectural projects in Vienna such as KunstHausWien.

events.title: Begins catalogue raisonné and archive
events.description: In 1999 Hundertwasser began writing extensive commentaries on his works and designed the layout and covers of a two‑volume catalogue raisonné, personally determining reproduction sizes and ordering. Building on a numbering system he had started in 1954, he oversaw the documentation of his oeuvre in the Hundertwasser Archive in Vienna, ensuring that his paintings, graphics, tapestries, and architectural projects would be systematically recorded.

images.caption: Textile design by Friedensreich Hundertwasser for Fernwärme Wien in Vienna, illustrating his characteristic graphic style similar to that documented in his catalogue raisonné and archive.

events.title: Death at sea and burial in New Zealand
events.description: On 19 February 2000 Hundertwasser died of heart failure aboard the Queen Elizabeth 2 while returning from New Zealand to Europe. He was buried on 3 March 2000 on his New Zealand property without a coffin and wrapped in a koru flag of his own design, with a tulip tree planted over the grave, closing a life devoted to uniting art, architecture, and the living earth.

locations.name_historic: aboard RMS Queen Elizabeth 2, at sea (Pacific Ocean)
locations.name_modern: Pacific Ocean, en route from New Zealand to Europe
